result: A virtually crosstalk-free two-color in vivo STED microscope was developed with ~8% EYFP crosstalk in the EGFP channel, ~5% EGFP crosstalk in the EYFP channel, and achieving resolutions of ~70 nm for Citrine and ~84 nm for EGFP.
evaluation: Claims C1 and C2 are directly supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B. The crosstalk percentages and resolution values are quantitatively determined from the data, demonstrating the technical achievement of the microscope design.

result: Spine head area strongly correlates with PSD95 area in both EE and control mice, with median spine head areas of 0.527 µm² (EE) and 0.462 µm² (Ctr), and median PSD95 areas of 0.158 µm² (EE) and 0.161 µm² (Ctr).
evaluation: Claims C3-C7 are supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 2A-B with appropriate statistical analysis. The correlation is demonstrated with Pearson's r values (p < 0.0001), and the median values with interquartile ranges are directly measured. The PSD95 measurements are consistent with previous EM studies (Harris and Weinberg, 2012).

result: EE housed mice exhibit significantly larger average spine head area and significantly smaller variance in both spine head and PSD95 size distributions compared to control mice, while average PSD95 area is not significantly different. Both distributions are log-normally distributed.
evaluation: Claims C8-C13 are well-supported by statistical analyses shown in Figure 2C-J. The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test demonstrates significant differences in distributions (C8), log-normal distributions are confirmed by Gaussian fits to log-transformed data (C9), and unpaired t-tests with Welch's correction show significant differences in spine head area (p < 0.0001, C10), variances (p = 0.006 for spine, p = 0.003 for PSD95, C11, C13), while PSD95 average area shows no significant difference (p = 0.54, C12).

result: Spine density is not significantly different between EE and control housed mice.
evaluation: Claim C14 is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B using Mann-Whitney U test (p = 0.68), indicating that environmental enrichment does not affect spine density in this experimental paradigm.

result: Spine heads and PSD95 assemblies show substantial size changes within 30 minutes (spine heads: ~20% growth, ~15% shrinkage; PSD95: ~20-25% growth, ~25-30% shrinkage), with weak but significant positive correlation (r = 0.15-0.39) between changes. Positively correlated changes (PC1) show ~3 times larger variance than negatively correlated changes (PC2), with EE mice showing significantly lower PC2 variance.
evaluation: Claims C15-C20 are supported by time-lapse imaging data and statistical analyses shown in Figure 3D-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. Linear regression demonstrates weak positive correlations (p < 0.0001, C17), PCA shows the variance ratio (C18), and unpaired t-test confirms significantly higher PC2 variance in control mice (p < 0.0001, C19). The interpretation of stronger positive coupling in EE mice (C20) is a reasonable inference from the PC2 variance data.

result: Large spines tend to shrink and small spines tend to grow (regression to the mean). The multiplicative downscaling factor for PSD95 area is significantly different between EE and control mice, while spine head size changes show constant slopes over time that are similar between groups.
evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The regression to the mean phenomenon is demonstrated visually (C21), and analysis of covariance shows significantly different slopes for PSD95 between EE and control at all time intervals (p < 0.01, p < 0.0001, p < 0.0001 for 30, 60, 120 min, C22), while spine head slopes show no significant differences (C23).

result: Large spine heads tend to stay large and small ones stay small over the 2-hour observation period, with no temporal shift between spine head and PSD95 area changes observed at baseline.
evaluation: Claims C24 and C25 are supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 4C, F, and G. The constant Pearson's r values over time intervals support the stability inference (C24), and the symmetric cross-correlation (~0.8) without temporal lag supports the absence of directional changes (C25).

result: PSD95 nanoorganization is more dynamic in EE mice than in control mice. In control mice, morphological changes increase with longer measurement intervals, while EE mice show consistently high levels of change (~80%) at all time points. EE mice show fewer perforated nanoorganizations and more clusters compared to control mice.
evaluation: Claims C26-C29 are based on visual inspection by three blinded scientists (Figure 5B-D), which is subjective and lacks quantitative statistical validation. While the trends are described, the authors acknowledge the difficulty in quantitative analysis of the complex nanopattern morphology. The lack of rigorous statistical tests and the subjective nature of visual categorization make these findings uncertain despite the careful blinded approach.

result: The coefficient of determination R² between PSD95 brightness and nanoscale size is 0.76, indicating that brightness is a deficient correlate of synaptic size.
evaluation: Claims C50 and C51 are supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A. The R² value of 0.76 is calculated from experimental measurements, and the interpretation that this represents a deficient correlation is reasonable given that 24% of the variance is unexplained.

result: Spines were mostly stable over 30-120 minute time periods, with occasional spine loss or appearance (likely filopodia without PSD95). Average spine head and PSD95 areas showed no large changes, and no directed changes from light-induced stimulation, phototoxicity, or blebbing were observed.
evaluation: Claims C80-C84 are supported by observations from time-lapse imaging experiments shown in Figure 3A-C. The stability is demonstrated by the relatively constant average areas over time (C82), and the characterization of dynamic spines as filopodia is supported by citation to Berry and Nedivi, 2017 (C81).

result: Environmental enrichment has multiple established effects on neuronal structure and function, including accelerating neuronal maturation, increasing synaptic protein levels, facilitating synaptic plasticity, increasing dendritic branching and spine density, and inducing spine formation. The visual cortex exhibits enhanced plasticity under EE conditions. PSD95.FingR efficiently labels endogenous PSD95 without overexpression artifacts.
evaluation: Claims C30-C49 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the context for the current study and are properly attributed to previous work. The claims about PSD95.FingR (C48-C49) are supported by citations to the original development and validation studies.

result: The observed spine head growth of ~20-30% is similar to changes reported in other studies over different time scales and conditions. MMF anesthesia may affect plasticity, and in vitro LTP experiments show temporal delays between spine and PSD95 increases, suggesting different regulatory pathways. The slot model proposes that AMPA receptor increases depend on activation of binding sites rather than increased PSD95 amounts.
evaluation: Claims C52-C58 are interpretive claims that contextualize the current findings with prior literature. They are appropriately supported by citations (Steffens et al., 2021; Kopec et al., 2006; Otmakhov et al., 2004; Meyer et al., 2014; Yang et al., 2021; Bosch et al., 2014; Compans et al., 2016; Herring and Nicoll, 2016). The speculation about awake state differences (C54) is appropriately qualified as speculative.

result: Synaptic scaling models predict multiplicative downscaling with increased activity. The narrower size distributions in EE mice may suggest better-defined synapses and more stable neural networks, analogous to decreased variability in firing rates after stimulation. The increased multiplicative downscaling in EE mice might explain the narrower PSD95 size distribution.
evaluation: Claims C59-C65 mix established knowledge (C59-C62, supported by citations) with speculative interpretations (C63, C65). While the analogies to firing rate studies and synaptic scaling models are reasonable, the authors acknowledge that their in vivo measurements under anesthesia may not fully match expectations from in vitro silencing experiments. The speculation is appropriately qualified but lacks direct experimental validation in the current study.

result: PSDs on large spines are frequently perforated. Nanocolumns of pre- and post-synaptic proteins are organized by activity, and receptor reorganization might alter synaptic strength independently of receptor amounts. The increased structural plasticity of PSD95 nanoorganization in EE mice might reflect increased synaptic plasticity after enrichment.
evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Stewart et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2018; Artola et al., 2006; Buschler and Manahan-Vaughan, 2012). The interpretation linking increased PSD95 nanoorganization plasticity to synaptic plasticity (C69) is speculative but reasonably grounded in the cited literature and the current findings.

result: Previous two-color STED microscopy of EGFP and EYFP suffered from high crosstalk (92% and 27%) requiring linear unmixing. The PSD95 nanopattern observed with PSD95.FingR is similar to structures in PSD95-EGFP knock-in mice and perforated PSDs reported by electron microscopy.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work (Tønnesen et al., 2011; Wegner et al., 2018; Arellano et al., 2007; Harris and Weinberg, 2012; Toni et al., 2001). These claims establish the technical context and validate the current approach by comparison to established methods.

result: Experimental housing conditions and imaging protocols are described. EE mice were housed in groups of up to 12 in enriched cages, control mice in pairs in standard cages. Imaging commenced 2.5 hours after anesthesia onset. The PSD95 area measurements are slightly larger than previous reports, possibly reflecting larger spine heads of layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
evaluation: Claims C74-C79 describe experimental methods and conditions, supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and appropriate citations. The comparison to previous measurements (C77) and the speculation about layer 5 differences (C78) are appropriately qualified and supported by citations (Wegner et al., 2018; Konur et al., 2003; Harris and Weinberg, 2012).
